cutting.intro: Trim lightly to keep Spathiphyllum wallisii tidy and healthy.
bullets: Every 2–4 weeks, remove yellow, brown, or torn leaves and spent blooms to reduce stress and keep growth neat.
Cut back leggy or damaged stems at the base with clean, disinfected scissors to limit disease spread.

support.intro: Structural support is rarely needed for Spathiphyllum wallisii in normal indoor growth.
bullets: Check every 1–2 months for loose or tight ties, unstable stakes, or leaning new growth that may need light guidance.

aeration.intro: Light topsoil aeration helps if the surface starts to compact.
bullets: Every 1–2 months, gently loosen the top 2–3 cm (0.8–1.2 in) with a stick or small fork.
Aerate when water pools on the surface or the top layer feels hard and dense.

cleaning.intro: Clean foliage and the pot area every 2–4 weeks to keep the plant functioning well.
bullets: Wipe leaves gently with a soft damp cloth, supporting each leaf to avoid tearing.
Remove fallen debris and rinse the saucer or pot rim to reduce pests, improve light absorption, and keep a tidy look.

humidity.intro: Humidity support helps this plant stay at its best indoors.
bullets: Refresh a pebble tray or run a humidifier 2–3 times per week to help maintain 60–80% humidity.
Watch for brown, crispy leaf edges or tips, which can indicate air that is too dry.

mulching.intro: Mulching is optional but useful for indoor peace lilies in peaty soil.
bullets: Refresh a thin 1–2 cm (0.4–0.8 in) layer of fine bark or coco chips every 3–6 months.
It helps slow surface drying and buffers small temperature swings near the root zone.

watering.intro: Water the Peace Lily as a repeat task based on soil and leaf cues.
bullets: Every 4–7 days, water when the top 2–3 cm (1 in) feels dry or leaves start to droop slightly.
Soak the soil evenly until excess drains out, then empty the saucer so roots do not sit in water.
Avoid small frequent splashes that leave dry pockets or constantly soggy soil.

fertilize.intro: Feed Peace Lily lightly during active growth.
bullets: Apply a balanced houseplant fertilizer at 1/2 strength every 4–6 weeks in spring and summer.
Add fertilizer to already moist soil, then water lightly to spread nutrients around the root zone.
Do not feed in winter, and avoid overfeeding, which can cause brown leaf tips and salt buildup.

repotting.intro: Check regularly and repot only when the plant is crowded.
bullets: Inspect every 6–12 months for roots at drainage holes, slowed growth, or water running straight through the pot.
Move up 2–5 cm (1–2 in) wider into a pot with drainage, not an oversized container.

inspection.intro: Do a closer hands-on inspection every 2–4 weeks.
bullets: Lift and turn leaves to inspect undersides, check the stem base, and look into drainage holes for crowded roots.
Take follow-up action if you find pests, mushy tissue, roots circling tightly, or roots pushing from the pot.

monitoring.intro: Do a quick visual review once each week between care tasks.
bullets: Look at leaf color, texture, new growth, and soil moisture, and scan for any pest activity.
If leaves yellow, wilt, spot, or growth stalls, adjust light or watering and inspect more closely.

careDetails.aboutPlant:
Spathiphyllum wallisii is a tropical evergreen houseplant grown for its lush leaves and white hood-like blooms. It forms a neat clump and stays compact enough for tables or shelves.

In nature, it comes from warm, humid tropical regions of the Americas, where it grows in shaded forest conditions. Its ability to handle lower light makes care for Peace Lily fairly approachable, but it reacts quickly to very dry soil, harsh sun, and soggy roots.

It usually grows best with bright, indirect light, slightly moist peaty soil, and steady humidity.

careAdvice.title: Rotate Weekly
careAdvice.description: Turn the pot about 90° each week to keep growth even and prevent the clump from leaning toward one light source.

careAdvice.title: Flush Salts
careAdvice.description: Once every 4–6 weeks, run room-temperature water through the pot for 20–30 seconds and let it drain fully to remove fertilizer salts that can cause brown leaf tips.

careAdvice.title: Divide Crowded Clumps
careAdvice.description: If the plant fills the pot with many tight crowns, divide it in spring by separating rooted sections and potting them individually to restore vigor and flowering.

careAdvice.title: Clean Leaf Surfaces
careAdvice.description: Wipe both sides of the leaves with a damp soft cloth every few weeks to remove dust, improve light capture, and make pest checks easier when caring for Peace Lily.

careAdvice.title: Check Mite Hiding Spots
careAdvice.description: Inspect the leaf undersides and where stems meet the crown, especially in dry indoor air, because spider mites and mealybugs often start there when growing Peace Lily.

soil.intro: Spathiphyllum wallisii needs a moisture-retentive but airy peaty mix.
bullets: Use an organic-rich, loose blend with peat or coco coir, pine bark, and perlite.
Aim for fast drainage with some water retention, so roots stay moist but not waterlogged.
Keep pH slightly acidic at 5.8–6.5 for reliable nutrient uptake.
Avoid dense garden soil or mixes that compact, and add extra perlite or bark if the mix stays wet.

water.intro: Spathiphyllum wallisii prefers evenly moist soil that never stays waterlogged.
bullets: Water when the top 2–3 cm (1 in) of soil feels dry, often about every 5 days in active growth.
Reduce watering in winter as drying slows; drooping with dry soil suggests thirst, while yellowing and sour soil suggest excess water.
Use a free-draining peaty mix and a pot with drainage so roots stay moist but not saturated.

soilPH.intro: Spathiphyllum wallisii grows best in slightly acidic soil, where nutrient uptake stays steady.
bullets: Aim for pH 5.8–6.5, using a simple soil test meter or lab-style pH kit.
If pH rises too high, leaves may yellow from chlorosis or nutrient lock-out, especially iron-related.
Lower pH with acidic organic matter; raise it slightly with small amounts of lime, adjusting gradually.

pruning.intro: Pruning needs are modest, but Spathiphyllum wallisii benefits from light cleanup.
bullets: Trim yellow, brown, dead, or damaged leaves at the base any time.
Remove spent flowers after fading to keep the plant neat and support new blooms.
Thin crowded growth in spring if needed to improve shape and airflow.
Use clean scissors or pruners and make smooth cuts close to the crown.

humidity.intro: Peace Lily prefers 60–80% humidity for steadier growth and cleaner leaf edges.
bullets: It tolerates drier air briefly, but prolonged levels below 40% can slow growth.
Dry brown tips, curled leaves, and stuck new growth often signal humidity stress.
Raise humidity with a pebble tray, nearby humidifier, or grouped plants, while keeping airflow.

sunlight.intro: Peace Lily grows best with bright, indirect light for steady leaf growth and flowering.
bullets: Provide 6–8 hours of filtered light or gentle morning sun; avoid direct afternoon sun, which can scorch leaves.
It tolerates partial shade and lower light, but growth slows and flowering often drops when light stays too dim.
In winter, move it closer to a bright window; in summer, keep it behind a sheer curtain or in dappled shade.

container.intro: This species is well suited to container growing.
bullets: Use a pot with drainage holes so excess water leaves quickly and roots do not stay saturated.
Choose a container only 2–4 cm (1–1.5 in) wider than the root ball to prevent slow drying.
Plastic holds moisture longer, while a heavier ceramic pot adds stability if foliage becomes top-heavy.

placement.intro: Place it indoors where light is bright but filtered and temperatures stay even.
bullets: Peace Lily is best as an indoor plant, though it can sit outdoors only in warm, shaded, sheltered conditions.
Set it near an east-facing window or a few steps back from a bright south-facing window, with 15–30 cm (6–12 in) of space for airflow.
Avoid cold drafts, heating vents, air conditioners, and harsh direct midday sun, which can scorch or stress leaves.

fertilizer.intro: Light feeding supports healthy leaves and blooms on the peace lily during active growth.
bullets: Use a balanced liquid houseplant fertilizer, compost-based feed, or mild slow-release formula.
Apply every 4–6 weeks in spring and summer at 1/2 strength dilution.
Reduce to little or no feeding in winter when growth slows.
Flush the soil sometimes to limit salt buildup in peaty soil.

winterCare.intro: Winter care matters because this tropical houseplant is not frost tolerant.
bullets: Keep it indoors at 18–27°C (64–81°F), away from cold windows and drafts.
Water less often, but keep the soil slightly moist, not dry or waterlogged.
Maintain 60–80% humidity with a tray or humidifier to limit brown tips.
Do not leave foliage touching freezing glass or unheated rooms.

propagation.intro: Division is the standard way to propagate this plant successfully.
bullets: Divide in spring or early summer when the plant is actively growing.
Separate clumps with roots and leaves attached, using clean hands or a sterile knife.
Pot each division in moist, peaty, well-draining mix and keep at 18–24°C (65–75°F).
Provide bright, indirect light and high humidity while new roots establish.

temperature.intro: Best growth occurs in warm, stable conditions without sharp temperature swings.
bullets: Keep it near 65–81°F (18–27°C) for active growth, with the strongest performance around 68–77°F (20–25°C).
Avoid prolonged exposure below 55°F (13°C); cold drafts and sudden drops can stunt growth and mark the leaves.
It handles brief heat above 86°F (30°C) better with 60–80% humidity, but frost or near-freezing conditions can kill it.

repottingAndTransplanting.intro: Repotting helps maintain steady growth and healthy roots in containers.
bullets: Move it in spring when roots circle the pot, drainage slows, or growth stalls.
Most plants need repotting every 1–2 years into a pot 2–4 cm (1–2 in) wider.
Keep the root ball intact, loosen only tight outer roots, and use fresh peaty, well-draining mix.
Water after repotting and keep in bright, indirect light while roots settle.

facts.text: The species epithet wallisii honors Gustav Wallis, a German plant collector linked to many tropical plant introductions in the 19th century. The species was formally described in 1877.

facts.text: Its showy white part is not a true flower petal but a spathe, a modified leaf that surrounds the flower spike called a spadix. This is a defining feature of the Araceae family.

facts.text: This species is notable among common houseplants for flowering in relatively low indoor light, although brighter indirect light usually improves blooming. That trait helped make it one of the most widely grown indoor aroids.

interestingFacts.didYouKnow: Peace lily flowers often turn from white to green as they age because the spathe begins photosynthesizing more actively during the later stage of bloom.

pestsAndDiseases.name: Mealybugs
pestsAndDiseases.solution: Wipe insects away with a damp cloth or cotton swab dipped in diluted alcohol, then rinse the foliage. Isolate the plant and repeat checks weekly until no new insects appear.
pestsAndDiseases.description: These insects gather in leaf axils and along stems, where they feed on sap and leave a cottony white residue. Infested plants may show yellowing, weak growth, and sticky honeydew.

pestsAndDiseases.name: Scale insects
pestsAndDiseases.solution: Remove visible scale by hand or with a soft cloth, paying close attention to the undersides of leaves and stem joints. Improve plant hygiene and repeat treatment with horticultural soap if young crawlers continue to appear.
pestsAndDiseases.description: These pests attach to leaves and stems as small brown or tan bumps and slowly drain plant sap. Symptoms include yellowing leaves, sticky residue, and reduced vigor.

pestsAndDiseases.name: Cylindrocladium leaf spot
pestsAndDiseases.solution: Remove affected leaves with clean scissors and keep water off the foliage during watering. Improve airflow around the plant and avoid crowding so leaves dry quickly after any splashing.
pestsAndDiseases.description: This disease causes dark brown to black spots on leaves, often starting in warm, humid conditions with poor air movement. Damaged foliage can yellow and decline if moisture stays on the leaves.

pestsAndDiseases.name: Phytophthora blight
pestsAndDiseases.solution: Discard severely affected parts and repot into fresh, well-draining peaty soil if the root system is still firm. Reduce watering frequency slightly, let the top 2–3 cm (0.8–1.2 in) dry between waterings, and never leave the pot standing in water.
pestsAndDiseases.description: This disease can cause water-soaked leaf lesions, stem collapse near the base, and rapid decline in consistently wet potting mix. It is more likely when drainage is poor and the soil stays saturated.
